newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major seizes on jobs data for election boost.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major seizes on jobs data for election boost.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major, on the election trail and fighting to claw back the opposition Labour party's 25-point lead, on Wednesday seized on a drop in unemployment to bolster his campaign.

Major, banking on the economy to convince voters to return him to power for a record fifth term in polling on May 1, hailed news of the 68,200 fall in the number out of work in February, saying: "Today's news is proof that Britain is booming."
The fall was the largest ever in the month of February and brought the number out of work to the lowest since October 1990.

"Unemployment is down to its lowest level for well over six years. Falling unemployment, stable prices, lower taxes, higher living standards, people's hard work has created a turbo-economy which is making life better right across the country.

"Only if we stick on this course can we be sure to make life better still," said Major as he travelled to a marginal constituency southwest of London at the frenzied start of Britain's longest election campaign since 1918.
But Labour's employment spokesman David Blunkett said the figures had been fiddled by the government.

"The Tories have changed the unemployment figures so many times that most people now completely discount them," Blunkett said, issuing a report showing how changes had been made to reduce the number appearing on the unemployment register.
"Yet even these fiddled figures cannot hide the major facts. One in five non-pensioner households have nobody working in them," he said.
Labour also increased pressure on Major to publish a potentially damaging report on government corruption before parliament breaks for the official campaign.

Major has decided that parliament will not sit from this Friday, which means a report by the parliamentary watchdog on standards will not be heard by members of parliament in time for it to be published before the election.

But Labour deputy leader John Prescott and minority Liberal Democrat leader Paddy Ashdown wrote to Major asking him to ensure the report -- which studies allegations that government MPs took cash in return for asking questions in the House of Commons -- is published before the election.
Sleaze allegations have surfaced repeatedly during the last five years, dogging Major's attempts to overcome his government's growing unpopularity.
The ruling Conservatives, suffering from a "time for a change" feeling among Britons after 18 continuous years in power, sought to fight back on Wednesday, choosing the battleground of law and order.

Home Secretary (interior minister) Michael Howard, attacking Labour opposition to controversial sentencing proposals in a government crime bill, accused Labour of "putting concern for career burglars and dealers in hard drugs above the need to protect the public".
The government has been forced to ditch the most controversial elements of the bill as part of negotiations on what can be handled by parliament before its dissolution.

Britain's best-selling newspaper, The Sun, which on Tuesday announced it had deserted the Conservatives and was backing Labour, on Wednesday drove the message home with a long interview with Labour leader Tony Blair.
Blair needs a swing of at least 4.3 percent compared with the 1992 election to give Labour an overall majority in the next parliament.
